All I know is that one minute I was driving home from work, then the next minute I was sitting in what looked like a comfy waiting room. The kind you see in dentist's offices. ragged ficus in the corner. As I glanced at a magazine lying open on the table, I could see the page where I'd torn out an article the month before while waiting for my biannual cleaning. 
 
 A moment later, a door opened and a man bustled in with a clipboard. He looked kind, but harried. It was the look of someone who had far too much to do and far too little time to do it in, but that would n't stop him from being as pleasant as possible in the few moments allotted. 
 
 At first glance he looked older, but as I studied him I could see that he was really only middle-aged like me. The wrinkles were premature, as if constant strain had taken a toll on him. These definitely were n't laugh lines. 
 
 `` Victor Campbell,'' he said. It was a statement, not a question. His voice was professional and a little clipped. 
 
 `` Y-yes?'' I stammered. 
 
 `` Right on schedule - but of course, they always are. Would you like a cup of coffee?'' 
 
 I gaped at him and the unreality of the situation increased. `` Would I *what? *'' 
 
 `` Would you like a cup of coffee? I can brew some fresh. My receptionist brought in some Seattle's Best today and it's quite good.'' He looked at me anticipating a response, and as I felt my bottom lip tremble involuntarily his gaze softened the slightest bit. `` If you need to cry, that's perfectly fine. Many do. You'll find tissues next to you on the table. Why do n't I make us a cup and we can go over the forms?'' 
 
 I still had no idea what forms he was talking about, but I worked on pulling myself together as he brewed the coffee. He talked while he worked. 
 
 `` I'm sure that this must come as quite a shock to you. Humans always know intellectually that it will happen to them someday, but it never really sinks in until it's so close that it stares you in the face.'' 
 
 `` Until what is close?'' 
 
 `` Death,'' he stated, as if it should be obvious. It confirmed the suspicion that had been forming in my brain for the last few moments. I sat back in the chair as if I'd received a blow. Slowly, the knowledge began to soak in and I felt the panic recede. I was dead. This was the afterlife. The afterlife looked like Dr. Turner's waiting room. 
 
 As if he could read my thoughts, Death explained. `` We try to make this first part feel a little familiar. It helps with the transition. We choose a place from your experiences to model it after.'' 
 
 `` So are you... I mean, you do n't look like the Grim Reaper or anything.'' 
 
 He smiled wryly. `` That old figment of human imagination. I never understood that. Is death really so frightening an idea? It's as natural as birth. I promise you, I have n't come with a scythe ready to cut your soul from your body.'' 
 
 `` Well, what *are* you here for?'' 
 
 `` I'm simply here to fill out the forms. I'm a glorified administrative assistant, really.'' He served the coffee in two mugs. He took the chipped one for himself and, without asking, put one sugar in mine. Just how I normally took it. It surprised me how much cream Death put in his coffee. Even though I knew better now, I could n't shake the idea that he should be... darker, somehow. More sinister. A drinker of black coffee, certainly. 
 
 `` Now, let's get down to it,'' he said, returning his attention to his clipboard. `` All the basic information is filled out when you're born and the Records department adds bits to it over your lifetime. Let's see - Victor Campbell. Age 46. Lapsed Methodist. Divorced, no children.'' 
 
 I began to picture what my funeral would be like - if Meredith would come, who would clean out my apartment. Shit. I hoped my brother Steve would wipe my browser history before my parents arrived. Awkward. A nervous, one-syllable laugh forced its way out of my throat. Death glanced up at me for a second, then continued reading. 
 
 `` So I think we have the first section completed. Now I'll just ask you a few more questions and you'll be on your way.'' He did n't say where. 
 
 For the next five minutes, Death quizzed me on moments spanning my entire life. I answered his questions with my cheeks on fire. Every small bit of nastiness I'd ever done in secret, every mean and uncharitable thought. But also every act of kindness. Every selfless motive and good intention. At last, he told me that there was only one question left. 
 
 `` Do you feel that you were a good person in life?'' His tone was casual, but his gaze was sharp. 
 
 My mind reeled for a second, reliving all the events that Death had just drudged up. I could have been better. Every missed opportunity jumped out at me. My throat tight, I finally spoke. 
 
 `` I have tried.'' 
 
 Death nodded and clicked his pen shut. Standing, he leaned across and held out his hand. Dumbfounded, I shook it. 
 
 `` Well, Mr. Campbell, the formalities are all completed and you may go.'' 
 
 `` Go?'' 
 
 `` Yes. That door, just there.'' He motioned. 
 
 `` Where-'' I closed my eyes for a second. `` Where does it lead?'' 
 
 Death's eyebrows went up a fraction. `` Why, to heaven of course. Or at least, that's how humans tend to refer to it.'' 
 
 Relief washed over me. `` Not to hell, then.'' 
 
 The tiniest smile touched the corners of Death's lips. `` No, Mr. Campbell. There is no hell. There never has been.'' 
 
 I walked across the room on legs that shook only the tiniest bit, and opened the door.

 It was usually not my business to intervene in other people's lifes. I had always been the calm type, had few acquaintances and hesitated to make new friends. And I did n't need any. I could talk to my current friends about everything I wanted to talk about, and ever since I had graduated from high school I did n't really care for strangers' stories. I had a girlfriend, Kate, a wonderful woman who was happy with life as it was, just like me. All of it appeared to go my way, and I did not want to change a thing about it, but I had idle time, and I liked the jacket. Could n't harm to get to catch a glimpse of its previous owner, I thought, while I unfolded the dry piece of high-quality paper. 
 
 *'' BY CHOOSING MY FAVORITE SMOKING JACKET'' *, the note said in distinct capital letters that looked a little insecure, almost as if they had been drawn by a toddler, *'' YOU HAVE PROVEN YOURSELF WORTHY TO INHERIT MY ENTIRE FORTUNE, MY LIFETIME'S WORK... AND MY VERY DANGEROUS ENEMIES. `` * 
 
 I winced again. I had n't been prepared to being addressed so directly, and I stared at the paper as if it had itself talked to me. I looked around, but could n't find anything special, somebody with a camera or the like, something that said `` Congratulations! You have been pranked!'' all over it. There was just me, my new jacket and the message, standing at a bus stop on one of those grey winter days, a common day in a common city, the city I had grown up and spent my whole life in. The streets were busy although not especially filled with people, a common day from the moment I had woken up. 
 
 I fastened up the jacket because I started feeling the cold. I held the paper loosely and tried to not think of it, but just standing there, waiting for the bus as I had done before suddenly did n't seem like the right thing to do anymore. So I read the message for a second time. Again, my hair stood on end when I felt like what was written directly addressed me. I looked around again, feeling a little foolish afterwards. What if that businessman with the newspaper sitting on the bench behind me had noticed my paranoid behaviour? He probably thought I was crazy. 
 
 And yet again I tried to think of something different. I started day-dreaming about what could change in my life if I actually inherited some stranger's fortune. Kate and I could move to a house at the countryside. We'd buy a nice car and I could myself drive it to work every morning. Maybe we could even buy a helicopter, and then we'd spend our weekends jumping out of it into the giant swimming pool we'd have in our garden. At some point, probably a short while after the dream had started to become excessive, the note must have slipped out of my hand, blown away by the slight breeze, and with it, the anxiety I had tried to suppress left. 
 
 I was woken up from my dream when somebody touched my shoulder from behind. 
 
 `` Excuse me?'' said the businessman from the bench behind me. He had a deep voice, of the kind that makes you immediately feel comfortable talking to people, but something was different. I turned around and, for a brief moment, looked directly into his light blue eyes. Suddenly, my heart raced. Had he observed me? He could n't possibly have anything to do with the note in my pocket. 
 
 `` I think you have lost something.'' He said, and as he opened his hand, I immediately recognized the paper. I grabbed it quickly, possibly rudely. I wanted to thank him but I could not make a sound. My mind raged. How had he recognized the jacket? It was black and definitely not noticeable in any way, I had checked that before I bought it. He looked at me, his eyebrows raised demandingly, and I understood he had posed a question, so I nodded. He still examined me suspiciously. In that moment, the bus arrived. The businessman prepared to hop on, but I just stood there, trying to vanish by sheer power of mind. 
 
 `` Do n't you want to get on the bus? I've seen you take it before, you know.'' said the man. He was observing me, and he had been doing so for some time now, I suddenly realised. 
 
 `` No.'' I pressed out. Then he left with the bus. 
 
 I quickly went to the bench where the man had sat. It was actually a well-hidden place that you could only see from the bus stop itself. I sat down and just stayed calm for a moment, partially because I wanted to calm down, and partially because I almost expected someone to come around the corner, searching for me. When none of both happened, I took out my phone. I hovered over the `` EMERGENCY CALL'' -button, but then decided to not make any premature decisions and dialed Kate's and my flat's number. 
 
 Nothing. 
 
 She was n't at home, that was all. Nothing to stress out about. 
 
 With shivering hands, I called her mobile number. 
 
 Again, nothing. 
 
 I just sat there and could not think straight. What the heck had I gotten her into? What had happened? Who had even written the message? All those questions were there, but I did n't find an answer to a single one of them. I had never been that scared in my life, not even back when Kate and I first dated. The fear of losing something, came to my mind, was much stronger than the fear of never acquiring it in the first place. But such thoughts, my mind revised itself, did n't help out of my dilemma. 
 
 I stood up from the bench, once more calling home. It beeped several times while I went unerringly towards the bus stop. When I arrived at the stop, I had a short second of relief as I heard Kate's voice, but it was only the answerphone. 
 
 `` Hi! This is Marc and Kate, but sadly we're currently not at hand. Call again later or... well, you know how this works.'' She never spoke like that in real life, she sounded almost like a stranger, her words felt weirdly empty even though spoken very nicely and humorously. 
 
 `` Hey Kate. I have gotten into something bigger, something I ca n't control.'' What I said sounded terrible. `` If you hear this, I am so happy that you are well. You need to leave. Now. They could get to you any minute.'' I had spoken with a lot of breaks, trying to find the right words, struggling to pronounce them over my shivering breath. That's why I could not quite finish my message before it was ended automatically. 
 
 I started dialing again, but then, while looking at my phone, I realized that it was terribly stupid of me to call her. They'd find both of us if they checked it. 
 
 I threw my mobile phone into the next trash bin and crossed the street. Nobody seemed to be following me. 
 
 When it arrived, I hopped on the bus, line 300, leaving the city westwards.

More shocks of thunder rattled quickly now in rapid succession, shaking the simple wood church on the hill. Some of the congregation was looking around nervously, perhaps fearing the rafters would cave in. I did not. I smiled at Pastor Williams and felt warm in the glow of his faith. 
 
 Cold wind howled for a moment as the church door opened, a heavy, solid wood piece. Heads whipped around in ungainly fashion among the pews to gaze upon a stranger standing there upon the threshold. He wore a black leather duster over faded jeans, a western style shirt, and boots that looked like they had trod too many trails. I thought it might have sandalwood on the handle, but set against the doorframe the stranger was too hard to see clearly. A dull red bandanna covered his mouth lightly, offsetting his icy blue eyes.  `` Of course friend, please, come in!'' replied Pastor Williams. If he was put off by the stranger's unnerving appearance, he did n't show it. `` All are welcome who come in peace in the house of the Lord.'' 
 
 The stranger gave a curt little bow to the Pastor before taking a deliberate step over the threshold. He closed those frost hued eyes for the briefest of moments and seemed to be collecting himself. Dust seemed to cling to his coat and boots, which struck me as slightly odd. Now clear of the doorway I could see that rain had been pouring down hard in those fat Texas raindrops that fell against my home's tin roof like an assortment of dimes and nickles. But the stranger I saw was bone dry, not even a hint of rain on him.

The stranger kept his gaze fixed on the Pastor. `` The sins of murder, deceit, lies. They compel me into this house of God on a night not fit for man nor beast.''

Old stories about the left hand being the evil side, the left-handed path, et cetera seemed to bubble to mind. The stranger's hands were held limply at his side though, relaxed. 
 
 `` Friend, if your heart weighs heavy you are welcome to take a seat on the pews and be welcomed among the congregation. We welcome all who --'' Pastor Williams was interrupted. 
 
 `` That's why I'm here Padre,'' the stranger snarled. `` You've welcomed in someone you should n't have. Someone who is dangerous, evil, malicious. In your little church you've allowed a killer who will cull each of you in turn, and you do n't even know it.'' An uncomfortable silence filled the room. The stranger remained stock still.

It was a quiet meditative warmth that seemed to make the air around his hand thicken like sunset on a gentle evening. I felt a measure of peace looking upon it like I have rarely felt since. 
 
 And that was when Mr. Jonathan Peters, local grocer and recent widower, stood up stiff straight like a lockjaw victim I had seen etched in a schoolbook. The earsplitting howl he let out between clenched teeth made the congregation wince back in a wave of terror. I could see those teeth now looked gleaming white and deadly sharp. Mr. Peters turned with inhuman eyes, his facial features distending into proportions more fitting of a mountain lion from a nightmare. He lept clear over the pews and made for the church door, running on all fours in a mockery of the human form. My God he was lightning quick and terrifying. It reminded me of spiders skittering across glass. 
 
 But the stranger was faster. In his left hand the silvered six-gun appeared flashing with an intensity all it's own against the lightning streaked night. He held it aloft and the gun blazed like Excalibur, all silver and fire. Mr. Peters, or what was Mr. Peters, charged forward with a terrible howl that promised murder. The stranger did not even blink as he squeezed the trigger five times. 
 
 My father shot guns on our land hunting deer or keeping the stray coyote at bay, so I am not unaccustomed to the sound of gunfire. But I swear to you with God as my witness the stranger's gun roared like a lioness protecting her cubs. Mr. Peters shuddered violently, twisted hard and then landed on the ground at the stranger's feet. His limbs were still flailing wildly in alien movements, joints working opposite their intended direction. Too-pale blood seemed to be coursing from his wounds. 
 
 The stranger took deliberate aim, paused, then placed the last shot of his silvered six-gun into Mr. Peter's head. The thing stiffened again, then stopped moving for all time. 
 
 Gunsmoke still curling behind him the stranger moved to depart. `` Vampires,'' he called over his shoulder. `` They're in the Good Book Padre, if you know where to find them.'' The stranger left out into the night with the storm on his heels.

*The bones of the ancients peeked through the desert haze, dancing in distance. Docks of Phoenicia, pillars of Greece, villas of Rome, all tucked behind the collective walls of merchant prowess. Walls that had - for a time - withstood the mighty Alexander. Walls that had opened to the Son of God. * 
 
 *Walls that now stood in the hand of the Muslim Turks. Heathens, it is said, that oppose the word of the Christian

prefixes.human_continuation:
God. Men and women, alike, that spurn the teachings of the lord. Blasphemous cur unfit to stand upon the ground once graced by our Lord and Savior. * 
 
 The dry desert wind had whipped sand against my bare cheeks. 
 Harsh, abrasive sand possessed by some spirit to make it a hell on Earth. 
 
 Too long had we been marching toward Tyre. Far too long. And since leaving my home - God, how I had missed Palermo! The opportunity to follow Benito Polsinelli had been too good to pass up. - The peace I had known as a boy was an exception in this world. This world split between half-truths and lies. 
 
 *Cur. The lot of them. And you are charged by God himself to reclaim that which is rightfully his! * 
 
 The words of Baldwin were still fresh in my mind. Charged with fury, hate, and lust for... power? What drove this man - all of these men - to cross swords, splinter spears, shatter shields, and cleave flesh from one another? I had longed for this adventure. Longed for the glory so often sung by the tales of yor. 
 
 Too long had I seen that this glory is not so. Polsinelli was an exceptionally intelligent man. He'd taught me much in the two years I'd been charged as his squire. I had no idea why or how I'd been chosen when we first began to travel. I was nothing special. Son of an artisan father, though I knew nothing of my mother. She'd passed during my birth, and my father had never spoken of her. Nor had he remarried. 
 
 No, I was nothing special. But I recall the day I first met Polsinelli purely because of how absurd I had found him to be. 
 
 A lone man riding a solid horse - both in its black color and muscular build - up the path to my father's villa. The sight of him dismounting, garbed in not but a simple tunic and trousers with a solid leather belt and plain dagger on his waste. His crest was the only way I had distinguished him as a man of honor. It was emblazened upon his horse's saddle: an Iberian shield of green with a single white stripe horizontally across its centre, two sheep touching their noses in the middle of this stripe, his family name below the shield, and his family motto - Pacem et victus - plainly laid atop the shield. 
 
 I'd asked in desbelief why he had sheep upon his shield. 
 
 `` Do you trust a wolf to watch your sheep?'' He had asked in a low but powerful voice. 
 
 `` Only a fool would trust a wolf,'' I had hastily replied, `` to do any more than what wolves do: kill and wreak havoc.'' 
 
 He did n't respond to this. He simply let out a muted `` hmm'' and walked to my father, who had been standing at the entrance to the villa. 
 
 I did n't hear the exchange between my father and Polsinelli. But, he had left that day, and my father had told me to ready myself for my new position as his squire. I had a week to get my things packed and in order. Polsinelli would return after that time and my training would begin. 
 
 Those first months were hard. God, they were hard. I learned, though, that Polsinelli was a man not to be taken lightly. Rarely did he speak. Rarely did he do more than point and give a handful of words as instruction. He expected me to use my mind. To think. To learn *how* to solve any degree of problems. 
 
 Evenings were spent with various texts - Herodotus, Livy, Plutarch, Socrates - that he would leave a note for me to read. Inside each of these texts were his own notes, scrawled in the margins. 
 
 Contemplations. Thoughts. Ideas. 
 
 Things that were not in line with the teachings of the church. Things that were not what were taught by the scripture. Things that would be considered blasphemous. 
 
 So I questioned him. And it was as if he had been waiting for that moment. The moment in which I doubted his instruction. His eyes glistened in the moonlight, and my education began anew. 
 
 I learned much from Polsinelli. And outside Tyre - gazing upon its shimmering walls, choking upon the sand of the Holy Land, drowning in the noise of thousands of Crusaders – Polsinelli taught me my final lesson. 
 
 That wind, hot and imbued with the vicious sand of the unforgiving desert, had bounced against Sir Polsinelli ’ s armor as he sat upon his horse. Baldwin was whipping the men into a fury, but we were behind the line with a small contingent of Baldwin ’ s guard. The men of honor in this contingent were to join Baldwin at the final moments before the battle. To lead the southernmost siege tower that had been built by the men of Baldwin ’ s army. We could hear the roar of the army gathered only a few hundred yards away, see their blades glimmering in the shimmering desert air, but only just so. Polsinelli rarely spoke before battle – rarely spoke at all, honestly – but he grumbled as he adjusted his sinister gauntlet. I proffered him the plain steel helm, dented and patched from use, and he grasped it while speaking. 
 
 “ Do you recall asking about my crest? ” 
 
 Even in the desert heat, I couldn ’ t forget that strange first encounter. 
 
 “ I do, sir. ” 
 
 “ Do you still feel that only a fool would trust a wolf? ” 
 
 I considered this, and responded truthfully, “ I do. ” 
 
 Polsinelli placed his helm upon his brow and turned to look back upon the city far in the distance. 
 
 “ I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves; be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. ” He drew a deep breath and turned his head back toward me. “ Do you recall this message? ” 
 
 “ Matthew, 10:16, sir. ” 
 
 He gave a brief nod, “ Correct. ” 
 
 A silence punctuated by the dull roar of the army in the distance filled a moment between us. 
 
 “ All of you are shepherds and each of you is responsible for your flock. Do you recall this? ” 
 
 “ That is the Prophet Muhammad, sir. ” 
 
 A second nod, “ Correct. ” 
 
 “ What does this have to do with my asking of your crest, sir? ” 
 
 “ The sheep is a symbol of peace. A symbol of what we must aspire to. I fight for that aspiration, ” he raised a gauntlet to the gathered army shimmering in the distance, following with his armored finger the figure of Baldwin slowly galloping the distance of the battle line, “ but what fellowship hath the wolf with the lamb? So the sinner with the godly. ” 
 
 He drops his hand to the aged neck of his horse, Lycurgus. Both were showing the wear of long years of fighting, travelling, and weariness from both endeavors. 
 
 “ My family crest was a wolf. My father was a wolf of a man. And a bastard of a man. But a lone wolf? That is only a temporary threat. Easily dismissed or disposed of. The threat of wolves is in their numbers. To nip and bite until their prey is incapable of fighting back. Bled, bit by bit, to oblivion. He knew that. And all wolves want a pack. A pack that they can lead. So they find – or make – a pack. And slowly they ’ ll nip and bite until they have risen to the top of the pack. On the bloody backs of those that they had once supported. ” 
 
 Trumpets echoed across the desert, and the other knights had begun to exit the camp. Polsinelli adjusted his shield and wheeled Lycurgus about to the exit. 
 
 “ What we are, now, is an army of sheep lead by a starving wolf. Sicily is an island of such sheep. Be their shepherd, not their wolf. ” 
 
 And with that, Polsinelli rode to his fate. 
 
 Tyre did not fall that day. 
 
 Baldwin would eventually conquer the city and “ expel ” the Muslim “ cur ”. 
 
 King Baldwin of Jerusalem. 
 
 But I had long learned that the leaders of the crusade were no more than wolves after the riches of the flock. 
 
 To follow them was death. 
 
 To resist them was death. 
 
 But to dissuade them? 
 
 It would take a shepherd.
